title: How a six-piece band started a tune and how choruses were shared
summary: De De describes the band starting together, the trumpet's two-beat lead-in, keys, and trumpet resting his lip while others take choruses.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Now when you started out, say they'd have a six piece band, I'll just choose for example, trumpet, clarinet, trombone, and a bass, and a guitar, and drums. Now, how would you play a tune in those days? Would it be the full band at first, or would it be one man, or how would you start off?
Oh no, we'd all start off together. We'd give the name of the piece quite nicely, most every man member of the band knew the number, melody anyway.

See they knew the melody, and whoever would lead the band was the trumpet player, he knocked off two beats. The band started all in one. Well name the key, you see, because the trumpet key, each instrument plays a different key. If a piano is in E flat, the trumpet would be saying B flat, each man knows his key. Well in other words, you make a variation in that key on the trumpet, they know what key you're in. Each one knows what key he is to play to correspond with the trumpet. That's the way that's done. Then two licks, you have to call it a number, and he'll lead off. That's what he's going to go right on the playing and then he'll right in there with him.
That's the way that's done. How many choruses would the trumpet stay up?

Well sometimes, he'd stay up one, some would take two, all depends on how strong the man was. Sometimes he'd play all through the pieces, three choruses or four choruses, whatever he would play. Most of the time they played three choruses.

They'd pick up, yeah, and then he'd rest his lip while the sax or the claret, who they featured in there, and then they'd come in on the last, sometimes the last half of the chorus or the last chorus, all depending on his lips. And some would stay up from the time they knock off till they knock out the band, play all the way through. But you feature one man sometime in a band at a time, whoever you want to take that chorus, that middle chorus. Or if there's five you want to play everybody take a heart, because they say take a heart, each man take a chorus, and the last chorus would go out. But the trumpet player would stay down mostly.
He's a full of a run-potato, that's all he is.
The trumpet player would stay down and rest his lip.
Well did they often take a heart in those days, as much as they do now? Not so much, no, no.

Not today there's a whole lot of solo and stuff like that. Some trumpet players picked up and put that horn out there left until the piece was ended. But if they played nine chords, no way to speak, he'd stay up. Strong though, you know, had to be. Now they'd just take down, wipe your lip, pick up again, get out for a few more hours and ride on again, continue.
